summary: Explains why choosing random values that resist a determined adversary is hard, points out pitfalls of ordinary pseudo-random generators, and recommends truly random hardware sources. It has been replaced by RFC 4086.

plainLanguage.summary: A password or a key is only as strong as the randomness behind it. This RFC explains why the usual pseudo-random generators and easy sources such as the system clock are not good enough, what to use instead, and how much randomness a given job actually needs.

questions: how to generate random numbers securely
subtitle: Why ordinary pseudo-random generators fail for security, and what to use instead.

tldr.problem: Cryptography depends on secret values that an attacker cannot guess, but most systems draw those values from a pseudo-random generator that an attacker can reproduce once they know the seed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC measures a secret by how many bits of information it carries, then shows where randomness leaks: clocks, serial numbers, complicated processing of a narrow seed, and picking a random slice of a public database. It recommends hardware sources and, where that is impossible, mixing several weak sources with a strong mixing function.
tldr.outcome: It also works out how many random bits different jobs need, from 29 bits for a modest password to 128 bits for a very high security key. The document has been replaced by RFC 4086.

today: RFC 1750 was an Informational document published in December 1994. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4086, which is the current guidance on randomness for cryptographic and other security uses.

sections.title: Why Randomness Is Hard
sections.content:
At the heart of all cryptographic systems is the generation of secret, unguessable, that is random, numbers. The requirement is for data that an adversary has a very low probability of guessing or determining. This fails if pseudo-random data is used which only meets traditional statistical tests for randomness, or which is based on limited range sources such as clocks. Frequently such random quantities are determinable by an adversary searching through an embarrassingly small space of possibilities.

The RFC's complaint is that a sophisticated attacker may find it easier to reproduce the environment that produced the secret quantities and search the resulting small set of possibilities than to locate the quantities in the whole of the number space. The result is pseudo-security.

Most traditional sources of random numbers are deterministic: they start with a seed and use numeric or logical operations to produce a sequence of values. A typical technique is the linear congruence pseudo-random number generator, where the N+1th value is calculated from the Nth value by modular arithmetic. Another is the linear shift register, where bits are introduced at one end of a register as the Exclusive Or of bits from selected fixed taps.

The goodness of these algorithms is measured by statistical tests. Carefully chosen initial values and carefully placed taps can produce excellent statistics, and such sequences may be adequate in simulations. However, they are clearly bad for use in security applications, because they are fully predictable if the initial state is known, and depending on the form of the generator the sequence may be determinable from observation of a short portion of it. With the linear congruence generator, one can determine V(n+1) given knowledge of V(n), and it has been shown that even if only one bit of each value is released, the seed can be determined from short sequences. Techniques are now known for breaking all polynomial congruent generators.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudo-random generator is a formula, not a source of surprise. If an attacker knows the starting value, or can work it out from a few outputs, every later value follows.

sections.title: Bits of Information and Adversary Effort
sections.content:
The RFC measures the strength of a secret by the amount of information it carries, where i varies from 1 to the number of possible secret values and p sub i is the probability of the value numbered i. If there are 2^n different values of equal probability, then n bits of information are present and an adversary would on average have to try half of the values, or 2^(n-1), before guessing the secret quantity. If the probability of different values is unequal, there is less information present and fewer guesses will on average be required. Any values the adversary can know are impossible, or are of low probability, can be initially ignored, because the adversary will search through the more probable values first.

The example given is a cryptographic system that uses 56 bit keys. If those keys are derived by using a fixed pseudo-random number generator seeded with an 8 bit seed, an adversary needs to search through only 256 keys, by running the generator with every possible seed, not the 2^56 keys that at first appear to be the case. Only 8 bits of information are in these 56 bit keys.

The most commonly encountered randomness requirement today is the user password. If a password can be guessed it provides no security. Cryptographic techniques are based on quantities, traditionally called keys, that are unknown to and unguessable by an adversary. The frequency and volume of the requirement differs greatly between systems: pure RSA needs random quantities only when the key pair is generated, the proposed public key Digital Signature Algorithm requires good random numbers for each signature, and encrypting with a one time pad requires a volume of randomness equal to all the messages to be processed.
sections.plainLanguage: The strength of a secret is the number of equally likely possibilities behind it. A 56-bit key has 56 bits of strength, unless the way it was generated throws most of those bits away.

sections.title: Four Ways to Fool Yourself
sections.content:
Clocks and serial numbers. Computer clocks provide significantly fewer real bits of unpredictability than might appear from their specifications. One version of an operating system on one set of hardware may provide microsecond resolution while a different configuration of the same system always provides the same lower bits and only counts in the upper bits at much lower resolution, so successive reads may produce identical values. There are also cases where frequently reading a clock produces artificial sequential values, because of extra code that checks whether the clock is unchanged between two reads and increases it by one. A hardware serial number such as an Ethernet address may also provide fewer bits of uniqueness than one would guess: such quantities are usually heavily structured, and subfields may have only a limited range of possible values.

Timing and content of external events. It is possible to measure the timing and content of mouse movement, key strokes and similar user events. This is a reasonable source of unguessable data with some qualifications: key strokes may be buffered, there is no standard method to sample timing details, and the amount of movement or the keys actually hit may yield less unpredictability because the user may provide highly repetitive input. Network packet arrival times can also be used with care, but the possibility of manipulation of such times by an adversary must be considered.

The fallacy of complex manipulation. One strategy that gives a misleading appearance of unpredictability is to take a very complex algorithm, or an excellent traditional generator, and seed it with the current value of the system clock. An adversary who knew roughly when the generator was started would have a relatively small number of seed values to test. Large numbers of pseudo-random bits could be generated, but the search space an adversary needs to check could be quite small. Very strong manipulation will not help if the adversary can learn what the manipulation is and there is not enough unpredictability in the starting seed. Blindly chosen complex manipulation can also destroy the randomness in a good seed.

The fallacy of selection from a large database. Another strategy is to select a quantity randomly from a database and assume its strength is related to the total number of bits in the database. Typical USENET servers at the time processed over 35 megabytes of information per day. Selecting 32 bytes from a random starting point does not yield 32*8 = 256 bits worth of unguessability: even allowing that much of the data is human language with more like 2 or 3 bits of information per byte, it does not yield 32*2.5 = 80 bits. For an adversary with access to the same data, the unguessability rests only on the starting point, at best about 25 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Four habits lead to weak randomness: reading the clock, using a serial number, running a clever algorithm over a narrow seed, and picking a random slice of a big pile of data everyone already has.

sections.title: Hardware Sources for Randomness
sections.content:
All that is needed for strong portable randomness is a physical source of unpredictable numbers. A thermal noise or radioactive decay source and a fast, free-running oscillator would do the trick directly, and any system with a spinning disk or the like has an adequate source of randomness.

The volume needed is not much. For DES the key is 56 bits and even the highest security system is unlikely to require keying material of over 200 bits. If a series of keys is needed it can be generated from a strong random seed using a cryptographically strong sequence. A few hundred random bits generated once a day would be enough, and even if the bits are generated as slowly as one per second it should be tolerable in high security applications to wait 200 seconds occasionally.

The distribution does not need to be uniform. All that is needed is a conservative estimate of how non-uniform it is, to bound performance. Two simple de-skewing techniques are given. The first takes the parity of a sufficiently long string of bits and maps the string to zero or one, which is robust across all degrees of skew and is trivial to implement in hardware. The RFC tabulates how many bits must be sampled: if the distribution is skewed 99 percent in favour of ones, the parity of a string of 308 samples is within 0.001 of a 50/50 distribution.

The second technique, due to von Neumann, examines the bit stream as a sequence of non-overlapping pairs, discards any 00 or 11 pairs, interprets 01 as a 0 and 10 as a 1. This completely eliminates any bias, at the expense of taking an indeterminate number of input bits for any particular number of output bits. The RFC warns that this analysis assumes the bits come from a single uncorrelated source: if overlapping pairs were used by mistake instead of non-overlapping pairs, the statistical analysis would be the same, but the output would be a totally predictable sequence of exactly alternating ones and zeros.

Existing hardware can be used. The input from a sound digitizer with no source plugged in, or a camera with the lens cap on, is essentially thermal noise; on a SPARCstation one can read from the /dev/audio device with nothing plugged into the microphone jack. Disk drives have small random fluctuations in their rotational speed due to chaotic air turbulence, and with low level seek time instrumentation, disk drives easily produce 100 bits a minute or more of excellent random data.
sections.plainLanguage: Real hardware is the best source. The amount needed is small, and the bits do not have to be perfectly balanced, because a simple rule can even them out. A microphone input with nothing plugged in, or the timing of disk seeks, both work.

sections.title: Mixing Functions and Strong Sequences
sections.content:
The recommended non-hardware strategy is to obtain random input from a large number of uncorrelated sources and mix them with a strong mixing function, one that combines two or more inputs and produces an output where each output bit is a different complex non-linear function of all the input bits. On average, changing any input bit will change about half the output bits.

The trivial example of a mixing function is Exclusive Or, equivalent to addition without carry. If two inputs are uncorrelated, the output is an even better, less skewed, random bit than the inputs, and since the eccentricity is never greater than one half the eccentricity is always improved except when at least one input is a totally skewed constant. The RFC warns that the calculation assumes the inputs are not correlated: the parity of the number of minutes from midnight on two clocks accurate to a few seconds might each appear random, yet combined with Exclusive Or the result would be zero most of the time.

Stronger mixing functions include the Data Encryption Standard, which takes up to 120 bits of input and produces 64 bits of output each dependent on a complex non-linear function of all input bits, and the message digest functions such as the Secure Hash Standard and the MD2, MD4 and MD5 series. The MD series produce 128 bits of output and SHS produces 160 bits. Mixing cannot stretch randomness: four inputs of 32 bits each with 12 bits of unpredictability in each cannot produce more than 48 bits of unpredictable output, even though the output can be expanded to hundreds or thousands of bits.

Where a series of random quantities must be generated, the correct technique is to start with a strong random seed, take cryptographically strong steps from that seed, and not reveal the complete state of the generator in the sequence elements. If each value can be calculated in a fixed way from the previous value, then when any value is compromised all future values can be determined. The least information revealed each iteration, the harder it is to predict the sequence, so it is best to use only one bit from each value.

The generator with the strongest public proof of strength is the Blum Blum Shub generator, which is also very simple and based on quadratic residues. Choose two large prime numbers p and q that both give a remainder of 3 when divided by 4, let n be their product, and choose a random number x relatively prime to n. The seed and the recurrence are s0 = (x squared) mod n and s(i+1) = (s(i) squared) mod n. It is always safe to use only the lowest order bit, and predicting further bits is provable as hard as factoring n. Its only disadvantage is that it is computationally intensive compared with the traditional techniques, which is not a serious drawback for moderately infrequent purposes such as generating session keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Mixing several weak sources together with a function that spreads every input bit across every output bit is the recommended fallback. The rule that matters: mixing cannot create randomness that was not there to begin with.

sections.title: How Much Randomness Is Really Needed
sections.content:
For a password that changes once a year, where the probability of an adversary guessing it should be less than one in a thousand, and where at most one try can be made every six seconds, the RFC judges that even if log files are checked monthly, 500,000 tries are plausible before the attack is noticed. To have a one in a thousand chance of guessing the password in 500,000 tries implies a universe of at least 500,000,000 passwords, about 2^29, so 29 bits of randomness are needed. To decrease the probability by 1,000 requires increasing the universe of passwords by the same factor, which adds about 10 bits. A one in a million chance would require 39 bits of randomness, and a one in 10^9 chance would need 49 bits. The RFC notes that in a real system the larger and harder to remember the passwords, the more likely users are to write them down, which adds risk of its own.

For a very high security cryptographic key, assuming brute force trial of keys is the best the adversary can do, and that a highly parallel processor can manage 10^9 keys per second, a minimum of 51 bits of randomness is needed to be sure the key cannot be found in a month. To be assured of safety against a meet in the middle attack, which can halve the exponent of the work required, the amount of randomness in the key must be doubled to a minimum of 102 bits. Since the questions of special purpose code breaking hardware and the safety margin are not settled, a good minimum for a very high security cryptographic key is 128 bits of randomness, which implies a minimum key length of 128 bits. If the two parties agree on a key by Diffie-Hellman exchange, only half of this randomness has to be supplied by each party, but since there is probably some correlation between their random inputs it is probably best to assume that each party needs to provide at least 96 bits worth of randomness.

The RFC's own security considerations section says only that the entirety of the document concerns techniques and recommendations for generating unguessable random quantities for use as passwords, cryptographic keys and similar security uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC works out the numbers: 29 bits of randomness for a modest password, 39 and 49 bits for stricter ones, and 128 bits for a key that must resist a serious attacker.
